analysis.one_liner: Bans pay-for-delay drug settlements, eases generic competition, and extends community health center funding.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2019 with 45 Republican cosponsors, the bill sat in two House committees and its subcommittees for the rest of the Congress and never received a markup or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for brand-name drugmakers to pay a generic or biosimilar competitor to delay launching a cheaper copy — deals known as pay-for-delay settlements. It would also make it easier for generic makers to get the brand-name samples they need to develop and test copies, let the FDA approve additional generics sooner in some cases, and extend funding through fiscal 2020 for community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, teaching health centers, and special diabetes programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay brand-name prices would benefit most: faster approval of additional generics and a ban on pay-for-delay settlements would get cheaper copies onto the market sooner. Patients of community health centers — roughly 28 million people, many in rural and underserved areas — would benefit from the funding extension, as would the clinics and the doctors the National Health Service Corps places in shortage areas. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers would also gain, from easier sample access and new legal tools.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits brand-name, generic, or biosimilar manufacturers from settling patent disputes with deals in which the generic filer receives something of value and agrees to keep its product off the market, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission with civil penalties up to three times the deal's value.

Lets a generic or biosimilar developer sue a brand-name maker that refuses to sell sufficient quantities of the approved drug for testing on commercially reasonable terms, and creates an FDA process to authorize access when safety programs (REMS) are being used to block sample sales.

Authorizes the FDA to approve a subsequent generic application before the first generic actually launches in defined situations, closing a bottleneck where a single first-filer could hold approval for 180 days without marketing.

Extends funding for community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, teaching health centers, the Special Diabetes Programs (including for Indians), family-to-family health information centers, and sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education through fiscal 2020.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drugmakers would bear the cost: they would lose the ability to pay potential competitors to stay off the market, could be forced to supply testing samples, and would face earlier generic competition on some drugs. The funding extensions also carry a federal cost, though they continue existing programs rather than creating new ones.

drawbacks.text: The settlement ban has carve-outs — payments for litigation expenses up to $7.5 million and agreements that simply allow an earlier generic entry — which companies could structure deals around, and the FTC could exempt other agreements it deems pro-competitive.

Approving additional generics before the first generic launches could dilute the 180-day exclusivity reward that gives the first generic challenger an incentive to litigate invalid brand-name patents.
The public health program extensions ran only through fiscal 2020, a one-year patch rather than stable long-term funding for clinics that plan years ahead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main provisions squarely target two well-documented ways brand-name drugmakers keep cheaper copies off the market — pay-for-delay settlements and withholding samples behind safety-program walls — and its cost falls on the companies that profit from those tactics. It is deliberately incremental: one-year program extensions rather than new money, and settlement-ban carve-outs that soften its bite. The strongest honest criticism is that it was a narrow GOP alternative in a Democratic-majority House and, lacking price-negotiation or Medicare provisions, addressed only a slice of the drug pricing problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, split among three subcommittees, and neither full committee ever acted on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on May 14, 2019, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee the same day.

It was subsequently referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and to the Judiciary subcommittees on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet and on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law; no further action is recorded.
Forty-four House Republicans cosponsored the bill, including members of House leadership and the ranking members of relevant committees, but no markup or vote ever took place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers came out ahead on this bill: it never became law, so they faced no new settlement restrictions from it. Patients were not left entirely empty-handed, however — Congress separately enacted similar provisions (the CREATES Act, requiring brands to sell testing samples) in December 2019 and extended community health center funding the same year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drugmakers; patients got parts elsewhere

for.name: Rep. Michael Burgess
for.role: U.S. Representative (TX-26); bill sponsor and physician
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 44 Republican cosponsors.

for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Greg Walden, Fred Upton, Steve Scalise, and Lamar Smith

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled a markup or action on the bill; it went only to subcommittees.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired, which received the bill's settlement-ban provisions, took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic chairs of the two committees of jurisdiction took no action.

industries.note: The bill outlaws the pay-for-delay deals and sample-withholding tactics these companies use to keep cheaper generics off the market longer, extending the period patients pay monopoly prices. It is the bill's primary loser.

Faster approval of additional generics, guaranteed sample access with a private right of action, and FTC enforcement against settlements that pay them to stay out of the market all expand their role and revenue. Their interest runs alongside patients, since more competition lowers drug prices.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net providers
industries.note: The bill extends federal funding for community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, and teaching health centers through fiscal 2020, sustaining care for millions of mostly low-income and rural patients.
